title: Hundreds Missing After Glacier Collapse Triggers Catastrophic Flood on Nepal-Tibet Border
excerpt: At least 95 dead and more than 480 travelers unaccounted for, including over 100 Indians, after a wall of mud and rock devastated the Himalayan border region.
body:
• At least 95 bodies recovered after a massive flash flood struck the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday morning, with authorities fearing the toll will climb significantly
  • More than 480 travelers are unaccounted for, including 105 Indians, 12 British nationals, three Americans, and 17 Malaysians
  • Experts say satellite imagery shows a glacier snout collapsed into the Lhende Khola river, likely triggered by a nearby earthquake, sending a wall of mud and rock through border communities
  • Flood alerts issued in India's Bihar and Uttar Pradesh as rivers carry the surge downstream into the plains

A massive wall of mud and rock collapsed into a river on the Himalayan border between Nepal and China's Tibet on Wednesday, triggering catastrophic flooding that killed scores of people and left hundreds of tourists missing in what is rapidly becoming one of the deadliest natural disasters in the region this year.

Nepal's prime minister's office said 95 bodies had been recovered by Wednesday evening, with 484 travelers reported missing — 391 of them foreign nationals. The disaster struck at approximately 8:30 a.m. local time along the Bhote Koshi River in Nepal's northern Rasuwa district.

A Wall of Mud Without Warning

Verified surveillance footage circulating online shows people fleeing moments before the mudslide engulfed the border area. Drone footage reveals the scale of destruction along the river, with entire communities buried under brown sediment.

"It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us. As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife's hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud."

— Keshav Prasad Baral, 68-year-old survivor, to Reuters

Houses, roads, and hydropower projects were swept away on the Nepali side. In Tibet's Gyirong county, a mudslide hit the major border land crossing, cutting roads, communications, and power links. Chinese President Xi Jinping called for an all-out rescue effort, while Beijing News reported significant casualties at the Gyirong border crossing.

Over 100 Indians Among the Missing

The Nepal Tourism Board reported that 291 foreign nationals remained unaccounted for, including 105 from India, 17 from Malaysia, 12 from the United Kingdom, four from South Africa, three from the United States, and one each from Australia and the Netherlands. Another 111 foreign nationals whose nationalities have not yet been verified were also missing, along with 93 Nepali travelers.

Eight South Korean workers at a hydropower plant in the area were separately reported unaccounted for.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with his Nepali counterpart and conveyed condolences. "India is ready to provide all possible humanitarian assistance to Nepal," Modi said on X. "Our teams are coordinating closely on rescue and relief efforts."

Glacier Collapse as Likely Cause

Scientists analyzing before-and-after satellite imagery from Planet Labs confirmed that a substantial portion of a glacier snout collapsed to initiate the event. Initial reports from Nepali officials suggested an earthquake in the region minutes earlier may have triggered the collapse.

"It's confirmed that a substantial portion of that glacier snout collapsed to initiate the event — probably including or entraining a fair amount of rock and sediment."

— Vikram Gupta, engineering geology specialist, Sikkim University

Earth scientist Dan Shugar of the University of Calgary noted the imagery showed significant snowmelt in the 24 hours before the disaster, suggesting warm conditions may have contributed. Nepal's snow-capped mountains have lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global warming, according to a 2023 United Nations report.

Risk of a Second Flood

Authorities warned that a blockage still lodged upstream on the Lhende Khola river could trigger a second flood. Flood alerts have been issued in the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which border Nepal, as several rivers flow from the Himalayas into their plains.

The disaster underscores the growing vulnerability of Himalayan border regions to climate-related geological events, a concern that extends well beyond Nepal's borders to communities across South Asia.
